## A coefficient is not an intervention

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
SPRUCE assigns warming and $\mathrm{CO}_2$. A slope on assigned warming estimates the effect of that assignment, in that bog, under the design assumptions.

An observational regression of taxon counts on organic carbon does **not** estimate "the effect of setting carbon to a new value", unless the [adjustment set]{.mark} matches the causal question.

[Randomisation]{.mark} is a design fact. Adding covariates is not a substitute for it.
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-causal-assigned.png){.sketch fig-alt="Hand-drawn contrast: on the left a die assigns x, which points to Y, marked assigned with a green tick; on the right a hidden red node with a question mark points to both x and Y, marked observed with a red cross."}
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
SPRUCE warming and $\mathrm{CO}_2$ are assigned; the slope answers that assignment in that bog. CA-SYS organic-carbon regression is observational—no $do(\text{carbon})$ without the right adjustment set. Covariates adjust associations; they do not recreate randomisation. This slide opens the causal hour. Simpson is next.

**Going further.** In the potential-outcomes notation, each unit has a response $Y(x)$ for every level $x$ it could receive, and the average causal effect is $\mathbb{E}\{Y(x_1)\} - \mathbb{E}\{Y(x_0)\}$. The regression contrast $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x_1) - \mathbb{E}(Y \mid x_0)$ equals it under three identification conditions: consistency ($Y = Y(x)$ for the level actually received), conditional exchangeability ($Y(x) \perp X \mid \mathbf{L}$ for an adjustment set $\mathbf{L}$), and positivity ($\Pr(X = x \mid \mathbf{L}) > 0$ for every stratum). Randomisation makes exchangeability hold by design with $\mathbf{L}$ empty; in observational data it is an untestable assumption about $\mathbf{L}$. The standard references are Hernán and Robins, *Causal Inference: What If*, and Imbens and Rubin, *Causal Inference for Statistics, Social, and Biomedical Sciences*.
:::

## Simpson {.center .pitfall-divider background-gradient="linear-gradient(160deg, #f7f4ef 0%, #f6d6e0 100%)"}

## Two hospitals, one survival rate {#sec-simpson}

François Giltaire, *Le paradoxe de Simpson*. A public-health report prints one number per hospital. Survival is 86% at A and 79% at B. The booking that follows from those two numbers is A.

![](figures/generated/sketch-causal-hospitals.png){.sketch fig-alt="Hand-drawn hospitals A and B with red crosses on the roofs, labelled 86% and 79%, and a stick figure between them pointing towards A with a question mark." fig-align="center"}

::: {.notes}
State the two overall rates—86% at A, 79% at B—and let the room say "choose A". Do not spoil the strata yet; the next slide breaks the table. Giltaire is the narrative source on the slide.
:::

## Inside each severity, B is higher {#sec-simpson-strata}

A takes mostly light cases. B takes mostly severe cases. Each hospital has 1000 patients.

| | Light cases | Severe cases | Overall |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 90% of 800 | 70% of 200 | 86% |
| B | 95% of 200 | 75% of 800 | 79% |

Light cases: B is above A. Severe cases: B is above A. The single published rate still ranks A above B.

::: {.notes}
Walk the table: A has 800 light and 200 severe; B has 200 light and 800 severe—1000 patients each. Within light, B beats A; within severe, B beats A again. Ask why the headline still favours A; the weight slide answers with arithmetic.
:::

## The overall rate is a weighted mean {#sec-simpson-weights}

The overall rate is the subgroup rates weighted by how many patients sit in each subgroup.

$$
\frac{800 \times 0.9 + 200 \times 0.7}{800 + 200} = 86\%
$$

$$
\frac{200 \times 0.95 + 800 \times 0.75}{200 + 800} = 79\%
$$

The denominators match. A puts a weight of $n = 800$ on the light cases, where the rates are high. B puts a weight of $n = 200$ on those same cases. That difference in [weights]{.mark} is enough to reverse the overall ranking.

::: {.notes}
Read the two displayed fractions that yield 86% and 79%. Point at the $800$ versus $200$ weights on light cases—the subgroup rates favour B, but the mix favours A overall. This is the mechanism CA-SYS will reuse without necessarily reversing the sign.

**Going further.** The remedy is standardisation: apply each hospital's stratum rates to one common case mix. With the pooled mix of 1000 light and 1000 severe cases, A gives $0.5 \times 0.90 + 0.5 \times 0.70 = 80\%$ and B gives $0.5 \times 0.95 + 0.5 \times 0.75 = 85\%$, so B is ahead once the weights are equal. In causal terms this is the back-door adjustment formula, $\Pr\{Y = 1 \mid do(x)\} = \sum_s \Pr(Y = 1 \mid x, s)\,\Pr(s)$, valid when severity $S$ closes every back-door path from hospital to survival. Whether to pool or to stratify is not a statistical question: Pearl showed that the same table can call for either answer depending on whether the third variable is a confounder or a mediator (Pearl, "Comment: Understanding Simpson's Paradox", *The American Statistician*, 2014). Direct standardisation in epidemiology is the same computation, with a reference population chosen in advance.
:::

## Severity mixes two hospitals that are not the same {#sec-simpson-dag}

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 9
%%| fig-height: 2.8
flowchart LR
  severity["Severity"]
  hospital["Hospital"]
  survival["Survival"]
  severity --> hospital
  severity --> survival
  hospital --> survival
```

Severity changes which hospital the patients go to, and it changes the survival rate. Pooling the light cases with the severe cases compares hospitals that did not treat the same mix.

The [paradox]{.mark}, in one sentence: a trend that holds in every subgroup can reverse once the subgroups are pooled, because the subgroups do not have the same proportions. The soil version is [the same arithmetic on CA-SYS](#sec-casys-confounding).

::: {.notes}
DAG: severity $\to$ hospital and severity $\to$ survival; hospital $\to$ survival. Pooling mixes severities with different hospital proportions—that opens a non-causal association. Read the one-sentence paradox, then jump to [#sec-casys-confounding] for tillage zones where weights shift the contrast without a full reversal.
:::

## The same arithmetic, on the soil table {#sec-casys-confounding}

![Observed richness by tillage class, in three panels: the mixed zone has both practices, the no-till zone and the tilled zone each have only one.](figures/generated/casys-tillage-zone.png){fig-alt="Boxplots of OTU richness for no-till and tilled samples, faceted by zone. The no-till zone panel has no tilled column and the tilled zone panel has no no-till column." width="96%"}

| Contrast | Samples | No-till minus tilled | 95% interval |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| All zones pooled | 595 | $+47.5$ OTUs | $-7.5$ to $+102.6$ |
| Mixed zone only | 226 | $+80.3$ OTUs | $-6.0$ to $+166.7$ |

::: {.notes}
Work through the two rows. The pooled contrast uses 595 samples and gives +47.5 OTUs. Restricting to the mixed zone, where no-till and tilled fields sit side by side, nearly doubles it to +80.3 on 226 samples. The hospital table had a reversal; this is the same mechanism without one, which is the more common case in practice: the weights differ, so the pooled number is not the contrast you wanted. Say clearly that both intervals include zero, so neither row is a detected difference. The honest sentence is that the practice contrast is imprecise here and that its point estimate depends on which samples you compare.
:::
## Why the two rows differ {#sec-casys-separation}

The CA-SYS zones are not a nuisance; they are part of the platform's design.

| Zone | No-till samples | Tilled samples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mixed | 114 | 112 |
| No-till zone | 171 | 0 |
| Tilled zone | 0 | 198 |

Two of the three zones contain only one practice. In those rows the tillage contrast is not [identified]{.mark} at all: any difference between them is also a difference between places.

::: {.notes}
This is a positivity, or overlap, failure, and it is worth naming. Within the no-till zone there is no tilled sample to compare against, so no amount of modelling recovers a within-zone contrast there. A regression with zone as a covariate will still print a tillage coefficient; it will be driven entirely by the 226 mixed-zone samples plus an extrapolation. The mixed zone exists because the designers wanted to test the spatial arrangement of practices, which makes it the right place to read the contrast.

**Going further.** Positivity requires $0 < \Pr(X = x \mid \mathbf{L} = \mathbf{l}) < 1$ for every stratum $\mathbf{l}$ of the adjustment set that the target population contains. Here $\Pr(\text{tilled} \mid \text{no-till zone}) = 0$ is a structural violation, fixed by the design, not a random zero that a larger sample would fill. Two honest responses exist: change the estimand to the population where overlap holds (the mixed zone), or keep the full population and accept that the answer rests on a parametric extrapolation. Weighting estimators make the problem visible, since the inverse probability weight $1/\Pr(X = x \mid \mathbf{L})$ is infinite there. Petersen and colleagues, "Diagnosing and responding to violations in the positivity assumption" (*Statistical Methods in Medical Research*, 2012), is the standard treatment.
:::
## The arrow pattern behind both tables {#sec-casys-dag}

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 9
%%| fig-height: 2.8
flowchart LR
  zone["Zone, and the soil in it"]
  practice["Tillage practice"]
  richness["Richness Y"]
  zone --> practice
  zone --> richness
  practice --> richness
```

Zone decides which practice a field receives, and the soil in a zone also acts on the community. That is the hospital graph with new labels: [severity mixes two hospitals](#sec-simpson-dag).

::: {.notes}
Point out that this diagram is an assumption, not a result. It says zone acts on richness through something other than tillage, which is plausible because soil type is unbalanced across zones, but the data cannot prove the arrow. That is the message of the DAG slides that follow.

**Going further.** In this graph the path practice $\leftarrow$ zone $\to$ richness is a back-door path: it starts with an arrow into the treatment. Pearl's back-door criterion says a set $\mathbf{L}$ identifies the effect of practice on $Y$ when no member of $\mathbf{L}$ is a descendant of practice and $\mathbf{L}$ blocks every back-door path; here $\mathbf{L} = \{\text{zone}\}$ qualifies. The identifying formula is then $\mathbb{E}\{Y \mid do(x)\} = \sum_{z} \mathbb{E}(Y \mid x, z)\,\Pr(z)$, and the previous slide shows that two of the three terms $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x, z)$ are not estimable. A valid adjustment set therefore needs both a correct graph and positivity within it. The reference is Pearl, *Causality* (2nd edition, 2009), chapter 3.
:::
## Roles on a graph {.center .pitfall-divider background-gradient="linear-gradient(160deg, #f7f4ef 0%, #e3efc8 100%)"}

## A confounder in the soil table {#sec-confounder}

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 9
%%| fig-height: 3.2
flowchart LR
  moisture[Soil moisture]
  carbon[Organic carbon x]
  taxon[Taxon count Y]
  moisture --> carbon
  moisture --> taxon
  carbon --> taxon
```

Both carbon and the taxon respond to moisture. The unadjusted slope of $Y$ on carbon mixes the carbon path with the moisture path.

If the [estimand]{.mark} is the association **at a given moisture**, moisture belongs in the model. If moisture is how carbon affects the taxon, moisture is a [mediator]{.mark}, and adjusting for it removes part of the effect you wanted. The pitfalls drawing is [three arrows, three estimands](#sec-arrows).

::: {.notes}
Moisture $\to$ carbon and moisture $\to$ taxon $Y$; carbon $\to$ taxon. The unadjusted carbon slope mixes paths. Ask the room: block moisture for "at fixed moisture" or leave it for total carbon effect? Wrong choice is the classic confounder–mediator swap—link [#sec-arrows] in pitfalls.
:::

## A mediator is a different question {#sec-mediator}

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.6
flowchart LR
  warming[Assigned warming]
  plants[Plant productivity]
  flux[Soil CO2 flux Y]
  warming --> plants --> flux
  warming --> flux
```

The top path is [indirect]{.mark}. The lower path is [direct]{.mark}. The **total** effect of assigned warming leaves plant productivity alone. Conditioning on productivity estimates something else, and only under further assumptions.

Write the path you mean before you add the covariate.

::: {.notes}
Warming $\to$ plant productivity $\to$ flux $Y$ is indirect; warming $\to$ flux is direct. Total effect of assigned warming does not condition on productivity. Adjusting productivity targets a different estimand under extra assumptions—say "write the path first" before opening `lm()`.

**Going further.** With nested potential outcomes $Y(x, M(x'))$, the total effect splits exactly into a natural direct effect, $\mathbb{E}\{Y(1, M(0))\} - \mathbb{E}\{Y(0, M(0))\}$, and a natural indirect effect, $\mathbb{E}\{Y(1, M(1))\} - \mathbb{E}\{Y(1, M(0))\}$. Randomising warming identifies the total effect, but not these two pieces: they also need no unmeasured confounding of the mediator–outcome relation, and no such confounder affected by warming itself (the cross-world assumption). Adding productivity to the regression gives the direct effect only under those extra conditions; if a soil variable drives both productivity and flux, conditioning on productivity opens a collider path and biases even the direct effect. The usual references are Robins and Greenland (1992), Pearl, "Direct and indirect effects" (2001), and VanderWeele, *Explanation in Causal Inference* (2015).
:::

## The explanatory target is $do(x)$ {#sec-do}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="64%"}
Johannes Hertel, *Linking statistics, computational biology and biochemistry*. The question he sets is the effect of varying the independent variable on the response, in an observational study.

Lewis (1973), as Hertel quotes it: an event $E$ depends causally on $C$ when $E$ would have occurred had $C$ occurred, and would not have occurred had $C$ not. Pearl (2000) writes the [explanatory]{.mark} statement as $P(\text{cancer} \mid do(\text{smoking}))$ and the statistical statement as $P(\text{cancer} \mid \text{smoking})$.

Confounder, selection bias, and mediation are defined inside that framework. A prediction of $Y$ from $x$ does not use the $do$.
:::
::: {.column width="36%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-causal-see-do.png){.sketch fig-alt="Hand-drawn contrast: on the left an eye watches a scatter of points, labelled see; on the right a hand-set slider, labelled set x and do."}
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Hertel's observational question is effect of varying $x$ on $Y$. Contrast Lewis's counterfactual wording with Pearl's $P(\text{cancer}\mid do(\text{smoking}))$ versus $P(\text{cancer}\mid \text{smoking})$. Prediction without $do$ is not the explanatory estimand—the fork and chain slides show why independence alone is insufficient.

**Going further.** Formally, $do(X = x)$ replaces the structural equation for $X$ by the constant $x$ and leaves every other mechanism unchanged. For a DAG with joint density $\prod_k p(v_k \mid \mathrm{pa}_k)$ this gives the truncated factorisation: the intervention distribution is the same product with the factor $p(x \mid \mathrm{pa}_X)$ removed and $X$ fixed at $x$. $P(Y \mid do(x))$ equals $P(Y \mid x)$ exactly when $X$ has no open back-door path to $Y$, which randomisation guarantees. Pearl's three rules of the do-calculus decide, from the graph alone, whether an interventional quantity can be rewritten in observational terms, and Shpitser and Pearl (2006) proved the rules complete. Lewis's counterfactual and Pearl's $do$ agree at the population level; the potential outcome $Y(x)$ is the unit-level version.
:::

## One independence, two causal stories {#sec-same-ci}

A [directed acyclic graph]{.mark} is what lets you check a correlation pattern against a causal theory. One pattern can belong to more than one theory.

The shared statistical statement in his pair of examples: $T$ is correlated with $X$ and with $Z$ whether or not you condition, and $Z$ is conditionally independent of $X$ given $T$.

::: {.notes}
Set up the puzzle: one conditional-independence pattern, two directed stories. Read the shared statement about $T$, $X$, and $Z$ without showing arrows yet. Ask the room what differs between fork and chain if $Z\perp X\mid T$ in both—the next two slides answer with arrow direction.

**Going further.** The graphical rule behind this is d-separation. A path between two nodes is blocked by a conditioning set $S$ when it contains a chain $A \to B \to C$ or a fork $A \leftarrow B \to C$ with $B \in S$, or a collider $A \to B \leftarrow C$ with neither $B$ nor any descendant of $B$ in $S$. Two nodes are d-separated given $S$ when every path between them is blocked; under the causal Markov condition, d-separation implies conditional independence in every distribution the graph generates. Fork and chain produce the same d-separation statements, so no test on observational data can tell them apart; only a collider leaves a distinct signature. The reference is Pearl, *Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems* (1988), and Koller and Friedman, *Probabilistic Graphical Models* (2009), chapter 3.
:::

## $T$ is a common cause {#sec-fork}

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 8
%%| fig-height: 2.4
flowchart LR
  T["T"] --> X["X"]
  T --> Z["Z"]
```

$T$ causes $X$ and $T$ causes $Z$. There is no direct arrow between $Z$ and $X$. Conditioning on $T$ leaves $Z$ independent of $X$.

::: {.notes}
Fork: $T\to X$ and $T\to Z$; no edge between $X$ and $Z$. Conditioning on the common cause $T$ blocks the non-causal $X$–$Z$ association. Students map this to age or severity as $T$ before you label confounder formally on Hertel's slide.
:::

## $Z$ acts through $T$ {#sec-chain}

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 8
%%| fig-height: 2.2
flowchart LR
  Z["Z"] --> T["T"] --> X["X"]
```

$Z$ causes $T$ and $T$ causes $X$. The conditional independence is the same as in the fork. The arrows are not settled by that independence.

::: {.notes}
Chain: $Z\to T\to X$. Same $Z\perp X\mid T$ as the fork, but mediation and control rules differ. Emphasise Hertel's line—arrows are not identified by that independence alone. Pair with [#sec-same-ci] as the setup slide.
:::

## The DAG is a set of assumptions {#sec-dag-assumptions}

Three assumptions are listed, before the arrows can be read as causes.

::: assumption
There is a DAG that is a causal representation of the system. A variable is independent of its non-effects given its direct causes. The only conditional independences in the data are the ones that DAG states.
:::

The second sentence is his [causal Markov condition]{.mark}. The third is [faithfulness]{.mark}. He notes that a complete measurement of every variable in the graph is generally impossible, so the practical question is which variables the analysis has to include.

::: {.notes}
Read the assumption callout slowly: causal DAG, Markov (independence given parents), faithfulness (only those independences). Incomplete measurement is the practical punchline—which nodes must enter the model? Everything after this slide assigns roles to a third variable.

**Going further.** The causal Markov condition states that each variable is independent of its non-descendants given its parents, which is equivalent to the factorisation $p(v_1, \ldots, v_K) = \prod_k p(v_k \mid \mathrm{pa}_k)$ and to "d-separation implies independence". Faithfulness is the converse: every conditional independence in the distribution is a d-separation in the graph. It fails when two paths cancel exactly, for example a direct effect $+\beta$ and an indirect effect $-\beta$; the set of such parameter values has Lebesgue measure zero, which is the usual justification, but near-cancellation makes tests unreliable in finite samples (Uhler and colleagues, *Annals of Statistics*, 2013). A third, often implicit, condition is causal sufficiency: no unmeasured common cause of two measured variables. Spirtes, Glymour and Scheines, *Causation, Prediction, and Search* (2000), is the standard statement of all three.
:::

## A third variable has a job {#sec-hertel-confounder}

The names, for an observational effect of $X$ on $Y$. A [confounder]{.mark} causes both. One example is age, between a disease phenotype and a metabolite. $X$ and $Y$ are then correlated even when they are unrelated. That is the soil-moisture diagram, [a confounder in the soil table](#sec-confounder).

A mediator sits on the path from $X$ to $Y$. Controlling for it reduces, and can remove, the correlation. That is [a mediator is a different question](#sec-mediator).

::: {.notes}
Confounder: causes $X$ and $Y$—age between phenotype and metabolite on the slide. Mediator: on the $X\to Y$ path; control shrinks the $X$–$Y$ association. Link back to moisture (confounder diagram) and warming–productivity–flux (mediator slide). Role determines adjust-or-not.
:::

## A variance factor touches only $Y$ {#sec-variance-factor}

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 8
%%| fig-height: 2.4
flowchart LR
  X["X"] --> Y["Y"]
  Z["Z"] --> Y
```

$Z$ causes $Y$ and does not cause $X$. One example is a [batch effect]{.mark}. $Z$ does not create a correlation between $X$ and $Y$. It can mask one. He would control it, by design or in the model, to recover power.

::: {.notes}
DAG: $X\to Y$ and $Z\to Y$ only—no $Z\to X$. Batch effects are the named example: they inflate noise on $Y$ without inducing an $X$–$Y$ correlation. Control for power, not because $Z$ confounds the effect.

The graph factorises as $p(x,y,z)=p(x)\,p(z)\,p(y\mid x,z)$. The only path between $X$ and $Z$ is the collider at $Y$, so $X\perp Z$. Conditioning on $Y$ opens it: $X\not\perp Z\mid Y$. There is no back-door, so $\mathbb{E}(Y\mid X=x)=\mathbb{E}\{\mathbb{E}(Y\mid X=x,Z)\mid X=x\}$ still carries the $X$ slope. The law of total variance splits the noise: $\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid X)=\mathbb{E}\{\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid X,Z)\mid X\}+\mathrm{Var}\{\mathbb{E}(Y\mid X,Z)\mid X\}$. A batch effect sits in the second term. Conditioning on $Z$ drops it.
:::

## An instrument touches only $X$ {#sec-instrument}

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 8
%%| fig-height: 2.2
flowchart LR
  Z["Z"] --> X["X"] --> Y["Y"]
```

$Z$ causes $X$ and does not cause $Y$. One example is a genetic variant. $Z$ does not create a correlation between $X$ and $Y$. It does not have to enter the regression. Some designs use it on purpose.

::: {.notes}
Instrument path: $Z\to X\to Y$ with no arrow from $Z$ to $Y$. A genetic variant is the example on the slide. Students confuse instruments with confounders because both touch $X$; check for a $Z\to Y$ edge.

The graph factorises as $p(z,x,y)=p(z)\,p(x\mid z)\,p(y\mid x)$. The definition of the conditional then gives $p(y\mid x,z)=p(y\mid x)$, which is $Z\perp Y\mid X$. So $Z$ does not belong in the regression of $Y$ on $X$. Marginally $Z\not\perp Y$ if both arrows carry an effect, because the chain is open. A confounder would add $Z\to Y$ and break $p(y\mid x,z)=p(y\mid x)$.

**Going further.** An instrument is used on purpose when $X$ and $Y$ share an unmeasured confounder $U$. The three conditions are relevance ($Z \not\perp X$), exclusion ($Z$ acts on $Y$ only through $X$) and independence ($Z \perp U$); only the first is testable. With a binary $Z$ and a linear, homogeneous effect, the Wald estimator $\{\mathbb{E}(Y \mid Z=1) - \mathbb{E}(Y \mid Z=0)\}/\{\mathbb{E}(X \mid Z=1) - \mathbb{E}(X \mid Z=0)\}$ recovers the effect of $X$; two-stage least squares is its multivariable form. With heterogeneous effects it identifies only the local average effect among units whose $X$ responds to $Z$, under an extra monotonicity condition (Imbens and Angrist, *Econometrica*, 1994). A weak instrument, one with a small denominator, gives a biased and highly variable ratio; Mendelian randomisation is the genetic-variant case on this slide.
:::

## A collider is a common effect {#sec-collider}

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 8
%%| fig-height: 2.4
flowchart LR
  X["X"] --> Z["Z"]
  Y["Y"] --> Z
```

$X$ and $Y$ both cause $Z$. One example is inflammation. Controlling for $Z$ induces a correlation between $X$ and $Y$. A study restricted to healthy people is the [selection-bias]{.mark} version of the same arrow: the restriction can create correlations that were not there.

Do not control a collider. The word for doing it anyway is [overmatching]{.mark}. The Bayesian-network notes call this arrow a v-structure, and they connect it to selection bias.

::: {.notes}
Collider: $X\to Z\leftarrow Y$. Conditioning on $Z$ opens a spurious $X$–$Y$ association. A healthy-only restriction is the same v-structure. Overmatching is the name for conditioning on a collider anyway.

The graph factorises as $p(x,y,z)=p(x)\,p(y)\,p(z\mid x,y)$, so $p(x,y)=p(x)p(y)$ and $X\perp Y$. Bayes' rule after selecting on $Z$ is $p(x\mid y,z)=p(z\mid x,y)\,p(x)/p(z\mid y)$, and $p(x,y\mid z)=p(z\mid x,y)\,p(x)\,p(y)/p(z)$. That joint does not factor into a function of $x$ times a function of $y$, so $X\not\perp Y\mid Z$. Once $Z$ is known, learning $Y$ changes the posterior of $X$.

**Going further.** The classical case is Berkson's bias (Berkson, *Biometrics Bulletin*, 1946): two diseases independent in the population become negatively associated among hospital patients, because admission is a common effect of both. The same mechanism appears whenever the sample is selected on a descendant of the outcome, including a filter on sequencing depth or a detection threshold on a qPCR assay. Adjusting for a descendant of a collider opens the path too, more weakly. Unlike confounding bias, collider bias cannot be removed by collecting more covariates after the selection; it has to be prevented at the design stage, or corrected with inverse probability of selection weights when the selection model is known. Hernán, Hernández-Díaz and Robins, "A structural approach to selection bias" (*Epidemiology*, 2004), is the reference.
:::

## A moderator changes the path {#sec-moderator}

$Z$ changes the causal path from $X$ to $Y$. One example is sex. Women and men may show different metabolite profiles in response to a disease.

The analysis is then a stratum, or an [interaction]{.mark}. Matching on $Z$ does not do that job, and the sample has to be large enough for the interaction.

![](figures/generated/sketch-causal-moderator.png){.sketch fig-alt="Hand-drawn axes of Y against x with two straight lines of different slope, a steep orange line labelled Z = 1 and a shallow blue line labelled Z = 0." fig-align="center"}

::: {.notes}
Moderator $Z$ changes how $X$ maps to $Y$. Sex and the metabolite response is the example on the slide. You need an interaction or separate strata, not matching on $Z$.

There is no new conditional independence to block or open. Write $\mathbb{E}(Y\mid X=x,Z=z)=\beta_0+\beta_1 x+\beta_2 z+\beta_3 xz$. Then $\beta_3$ is the change in the $X$ slope per unit of $Z$. Matching on $Z$ mixes the stratum slopes; it does not estimate $\beta_3$. A confounder is a fork you condition on to recover $X\perp Y\mid Z$ under the null of no effect. A collider is the opposite pattern, $X\perp Y$ until you condition. A moderator is neither.

**Going further.** Effect modification is scale-dependent: on a log link, $\beta_3 = 0$ means the rate ratio is the same in each stratum of $Z$, yet the difference in $\mu$ can still differ between strata, and the reverse holds on the identity scale. So "no interaction" must always name the link $g$. VanderWeele distinguishes effect modification (the effect of $X$ varies across levels of $Z$, with $Z$ merely observed) from causal interaction (joint intervention on $X$ and $Z$), which needs $Z$ itself to be unconfounded. Power is the practical limit: with a balanced binary $Z$, the standard error of $\beta_3$ is roughly twice that of a main effect, so detecting an interaction of the same size takes about four times the sample (Gelman, Hill and Vehtari, *Regression and Other Stories*, 2020).
:::

## Adjust what the role requires {#sec-adjust-rules}

The control list, for an explanatory analysis.

::: {.incremental}
- A confounder: control it, by matching or in the model, or the interpretation is wrong.

- A collider: leave it out.

- A variance factor: control it, for power.

- A mediator: leave it out, unless the question is that path.

- A moderator: an interaction or a stratum, not a match alone.

- An instrument: optional. Some designs are built around it.
:::


::: {.notes}
Step the six fragments as a control checklist: confounder in, collider out, variance factor in for power, mediator out unless that path is the estimand, moderator needs interaction, instrument optional. About one minute if you step each line—pause after collider versus confounder because that pair is what exams test.
:::

## Which of these is age, and which is diet? {#sec-parkinson}

The discussion, left as a discussion. Parkinson's disease and the blood metabolome. The candidates he writes down: age, sex, BMI, kidney function, exercise, diet, smoking, Parkinson's medication, and other medication.

The question he asks is which of those you would control, and which assumption that control uses. The six labels under his sketch are confounder, variance factor, collider, instrument, mediator, and moderator.

::: {.notes}
Leave it conversational: Parkinson's metabolome with age, sex, BMI, kidney function, exercise, diet, smoking, medications listed on the slide. Ask the room to tag each candidate with one of Hertel's six roles and to say what happens if they adjust blindly. No single answer key on the slide—that is intentional.
:::

## The simulated association matches only if the arrow is real {#sec-sem-iff}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
The closing slide is a [structural equation model]{.mark} on a DAG: host factors, a microbiome layer, community secretion, and the host metabolome. The sentence drawn from it:

> "in silico association statistics" will correlate with "in vivo association statistics" if and only if the microbiome is causal for a metabolite in the host.

An association computed from the model tracks the association in the host when that causal arrow is the one in the diagram.
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-causal-sem-iff.png){.sketch fig-alt="Hand-drawn two-row comparison: when an arrow joins microbiome M to metabolite m, the in silico and in vivo panels show the same slope and get a green tick; when the arrow is crossed out, one panel is sloped and the other flat, with a red cross."}
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Read the quoted if-and-only-if carefully: in silico association tracks in vivo association only when the microbiome truly causes the metabolite in the host. The SEM DAG on the slide is host factors, microbiome, secretion, metabolome—association is not direction. This is the bridge to network search limits later.

**Going further.** A structural equation model writes each node as a function of its parents plus an independent error, $V_k = f_k(\mathrm{pa}_k, \varepsilon_k)$; in the linear case, the covariance between two nodes is the sum over connecting open paths of the products of path coefficients (Wright's path-tracing rules, 1921). The if-and-only-if then has a precise reading: the in silico statistic reproduces the in vivo one when the path through the microbiome carries the association, and agreement can fail either because that coefficient is zero or because another open path, such as host diet acting on both, contributes. Even a perfect match only shows consistency with the graph, not that the graph is the unique one; equivalent models with reversed arrows fit the same covariance. Bollen, *Structural Equations with Latent Variables* (1989), covers identification and fit for this model class.
:::

## Sensitivity is the causal report {#sec-causal-sensitivity}

For an observational claim, say what would have to be true for the conclusion to change:

- a [missing confounder]{.mark} associated with both $x$ and $Y$ at a stated strength
- a different adjustment set from the same diagram
- a different family, if the mean is sensitive to the variance assumption
- a different prior, if the fit is Bayesian and the sample is small

SPRUCE still needs a sensitivity story for the chamber itself: the design page monitors chamberless areas because the enclosure is not identical to an open bog. The pitfalls card is [show that the conclusion can move](#sec-sensitivity).

::: {.notes}
Observational claims need explicit what-ifs: unmeasured confounder strength, alternate adjustment sets, family change, prior change for small Bayesian fits. SPRUCE chamberless plots are the designed sensitivity for enclosure versus open bog—cite the design page line on the slide. Link [#sec-sensitivity] in pitfalls for the reporting habit.

**Going further.** The first bullet has a closed-form answer. For an observed risk ratio $RR$ (or a rate ratio from a log-link GLM), the E-value $RR + \sqrt{RR(RR - 1)}$ is the minimum strength of association, on the risk-ratio scale, that an unmeasured confounder would need with both treatment and outcome to move the estimate to the null, conditional on the measured covariates (VanderWeele and Ding, *Annals of Internal Medicine*, 2017). It rests on the Ding–VanderWeele bounding factor, which makes no assumption about the confounder's distribution, so it is conservative. Rosenbaum's sensitivity parameter $\Gamma$ plays the same role for matched designs: it bounds how far the odds of treatment can differ between two matched units because of an unobserved covariate (Rosenbaum, *Observational Studies*, 2002). For the Bayesian bullet, the analogue is to report the posterior under at least two priors and say whether the decision changes.
:::

## Searching a graph {.center .pitfall-divider background-gradient="linear-gradient(160deg, #f7f4ef 0%, #d4f0f6 100%)"}

## A direct link is not a direction {#sec-bn-direction}

The Bayesian-network course notes separate two graphs. A [dependency network]{.mark} joins two variables that still share a statistical relationship once the others are accounted for. That removes indirect co-variation. It does not say which way the link runs.

A regulatory direction needs a further claim, in the notes' words: a change in $X$ produces a change in $Y$, and a change in $Y$ does not change $X$. That is the same gap as Hertel's fork and chain, [one independence, two causal stories](#sec-same-ci).

::: {.notes}
Dependency networks remove indirect association once other variables are accounted for—they do not orient edges. Regulatory direction needs asymmetry under intervention, as the notes quote. Tie back to [#sec-same-ci]: statistics alone did not pick fork versus chain.

**Going further.** For Gaussian data the dependency network is the Gaussian graphical model: an edge $A - B$ is absent exactly when the partial correlation of $A$ and $B$ given all other variables is zero, which is a zero in the precision matrix $\Sigma^{-1}$. The graphical lasso (Friedman, Hastie and Tibshirani, *Biostatistics*, 2008) estimates a sparse $\Sigma^{-1}$ when the number of variables exceeds the sample size. This undirected graph is the moral graph of any DAG that generated the data: it contains every DAG edge plus an edge between co-parents of a collider, so it can show a link that no causal arrow supports. For compositional counts such as 16S data, partial correlations on raw proportions are biased by the sum constraint, which is why methods such as SPIEC-EASI work on log-ratios first (Kurtz and colleagues, *PLoS Computational Biology*, 2015). Lauritzen, *Graphical Models* (1996), is the reference text.
:::

## Three graphs, one distribution {#sec-cpdag}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
With $Z$ between $X$ and $Y$, and no direct arrow from $X$ to $Y$, the notes count four directed acyclic graphs. Three of them encode the same conditional independences. Those three are one [Markov equivalence class]{.mark}, drawn as a completed partially directed acyclic graph: an edge is directed only when the direction is identified, and left undirected when it is not.

Statistics on the observational distribution will not separate the three. The notes' next step is a causal analysis.
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-causal-cpdag.png){.sketch fig-alt="Hand-drawn graphs on X, Z and Y: three chains and forks boxed together in blue as one class, and beside them in orange the collider X to Z from Y, standing alone."}
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
With $Z$ between $X$ and $Y$ and no $X\to Y$, four DAGs collapse to one Markov equivalence class of three—CPDAG leaves some edges undirected. Observational data cannot pick among the three; the notes point to causal analysis next. Knock-out and time series are the two escapes on the following slides.

**Going further.** Verma and Pearl (1990) proved that two DAGs are Markov equivalent exactly when they have the same skeleton and the same v-structures, that is the same unshielded colliders $A \to B \leftarrow C$ with $A$ and $C$ non-adjacent. Here the three graphs without a collider at $Z$ share skeleton $X - Z - Y$ and have no v-structure, while $X \to Z \leftarrow Y$ has one, so it sits alone in its class. The CPDAG (or essential graph) directs an edge when every member of the class agrees on it; Meek's rules (1995) propagate those compelled orientations from the v-structures without creating a new collider or a cycle. With linear structural equations and non-Gaussian errors the class can shrink to one graph (LiNGAM, Shimizu and colleagues, 2006), which is one way extra assumptions buy direction.
:::

## A knock-out supplies the direction {#sec-knockout}

When the graph was not drawn by an expert, the notes' first source of direction is a [perturbation]{.mark}. If knocking out $X$ changes $Y$, the notes write $X \to Y$. They identify that experiment with the $do$-operator.

It is empirical, and it does not need a fitted network. It is a wet-lab result. Orienting a whole network this way needs many perturbations, which the notes say does not scale.

::: {.notes}
Perturbation first: knock out $X$, watch $Y$, write $X\to Y$ and link to $do(X)$. Wet-lab empirical direction without fitting a network—but scaling to whole networks needs many knockouts, which the notes dismiss. Contrast with passive observational equivalence on the previous slide.

**Going further.** A perfect intervention on $X$ cuts every arrow into $X$, so comparing the distribution of $Y$ with and without the knock-out tests $X \to Y$ against $Y \to X$ directly; it also distinguishes members of the same Markov equivalence class. Eberhardt, Glymour and Scheines (2005) showed that $p - 1$ single-variable interventions are sufficient, and in the worst case necessary, to orient every edge of a $p$-node graph, which is the "does not scale" remark in formal terms. Knock-outs are rarely perfect: compensation, off-target effects and incomplete silencing make them soft interventions, which change $p(x \mid \mathrm{pa}_X)$ rather than fix $X$. Mixing observational and interventional data under a known intervention target is what the GIES algorithm of Hauser and Bühlmann (*JMLR*, 2012) does.
:::

## Time supplies the direction {#sec-dbn}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
The other source in the notes is a series. The regression is the dependency-network regression, moved forward one time step.

::: model
$$
Y(t+1) \approx a_1 X_1(t) + \cdots + a_k X_k(t).
$$
:::

If $a_i \ne 0$, then $X_i$ regulates $Y$ from one time to the next. The notes call this a [dynamic Bayesian network]{.mark}: an initial state, the same transition from time to time, and the chain unrolled.
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-causal-dbn.png){.sketch fig-alt="Hand-drawn nodes X1, X2 and Y at time t and again at time t plus 1, with blue arrows from X1 and X2 at time t to Y at time t plus 1, along a time axis."}
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Read the model callout: $Y(t+1)$ regressed on $X_1(t),\ldots,X_k(t)$. Non-zero $a_i$ means $X_i$ regulates $Y$ forward in time—direction from lag, not from partial correlation alone. Dynamic BN unrolls the same transition; link to flux time series only if you stay within the slide's regression wording.

**Going further.** Testing $a_i = 0$ in this lagged regression is Granger causality (Granger, *Econometrica*, 1969): $X_i$ Granger-causes $Y$ when its past improves the prediction of $Y$ beyond the past of every other included series. It is a statement about prediction, and it equals a causal claim only when all common drivers are in the regression, the sampling interval is shorter than the causal lag, and there is no instantaneous effect within a time step; a slow, unmeasured seasonal driver produces spurious lags. A dynamic Bayesian network adds the assumptions that the transition is first-order Markov and stationary, so one two-slice graph describes the whole series (Murphy, *Dynamic Bayesian Networks*, PhD thesis, 2002). Because arrows only point forward in time, the acyclicity restriction is lifted across slices, which is how feedback loops re-enter.
:::

## Tests, or a score, when nobody states the graph {#sec-bn-search}

The notes' three searches, for the case with no expert graph.

::: {.incremental}
- Constraint-based: test a conditional independence. If the test rejects independence, the nodes are joined.

- Score-based: give each candidate graph a score for how well it describes the data, and maximise the score.

- Hybrid: learn the [skeleton]{.mark} from the constraints, then refine it with a score.
:::


Marco Scutari's benchmark, as the notes report it, for the developer of `bnlearn`: at small samples the constraint-based algorithms were more accurate than the score-based ones, and as accurate as the hybrids. Tabu search, a score-based method, was faster than the constraint-based algorithms and faster than simulated annealing.

::: {.notes}
Step the three items: constraint-based joins nodes when independence tests fail; score-based maximises a graph score; hybrid skeleton then score. The figure on the next slide is the same three families, with algorithm names printed on the nodes. These learn association structure under DAG assumptions, not causation by default.

**Going further.** The reference constraint-based method is the PC algorithm (Spirtes and Glymour, 1991): start from the complete undirected graph, delete an edge $A - B$ as soon as some subset $S$ of the current neighbours makes $A \perp B \mid S$ pass the test, then orient the v-structures and apply Meek's rules. Its output is a CPDAG, and it is consistent as $n \to \infty$ under causal Markov, faithfulness, causal sufficiency and correct tests; Kalisch and Bühlmann (*JMLR*, 2007) extended this to sparse high-dimensional Gaussian graphs. Score-based methods maximise a decomposable score such as BIC or BDe, and the greedy equivalence search of Chickering (2002) is consistent under the same assumptions. Searching all DAGs exactly is NP-hard, which is why hill-climbing and tabu are heuristics. FCI relaxes causal sufficiency and returns a partial ancestral graph that admits latent confounders.
:::

## Where the searches landed {#sec-bn-families}

![Three overlapping families: constraint-based, hybrid, and score-based, with gene labels and the algorithm that returned each one.](figures/sources/constraint-vs-score.jpg){fig-alt="Three overlapping circles labelled constraint-based, hybrid, and score-based. Several genes, including PRODH and SLC13A5, are tied to constraint-based searches such as GS-RSMAX and MMPC-RSMAX. LPL is tied to the score-based search GS-HC. SEMA3E is tied to hybrid searches MMPC-HC-MMHC and MMPC-TS-MMHC." width="78%"}

The labels are the searches, not a new biological claim.

- Constraint-based circle: labels such as GS-RSMAX and MMPC-RSMAX
- Score-based circle: LPL, labelled GS-HC
- Hybrid boundary: SEMA3E, labelled MMPC-HC-MMHC and MMPC-TS-MMHC

::: {.notes}
Do not interpret the gene names. Point at LPL in the score-based circle and at SEMA3E on the hybrid boundary. Read the labels as printed. The speed remark on the previous slide is about tabu search, the TS in MMPC-TS-MMHC.
:::

## A searched graph is still a DAG {#sec-bn-caveats}

The notes' limits on that search. The graph has no cycles, so a [feedback loop]{.mark} or a self-regulation is outside it. Adding observations can change the direction of an edge. A network of thousands of nodes is too large to enumerate, and the search then needs a heuristic.

The two implementations they name are `bnlearn` in R and `PyAgrum` in Python.

![](figures/generated/sketch-causal-no-cycle.png){.sketch fig-alt="Hand-drawn contrast: a red loop of arrows from X to Y to Z and back to X, marked loop with a cross, beside a green acyclic graph on the same three nodes marked DAG with a tick." fig-align="center"}

::: {.notes}
Close the limits first: no cycles, so feedback is out; more data can flip an edge; thousands of nodes need a heuristic. The next slide is only the two implementations. Causal claims still need design, $do$, or a perturbation. Thirty seconds.

**Going further.** The number of DAGs on $p$ labelled nodes grows super-exponentially (Robinson's recursion gives about $4.2 \times 10^{18}$ for $p = 10$), so exhaustive search stops at a few dozen nodes even with dynamic programming. Edge flips with more data are expected rather than alarming: the score difference between equivalent orientations is zero, and between near-equivalent ones it is small, so the bootstrap edge-frequency of Friedman, Goldszmidt and Wyner (1999), available as `boot.strength()` in `bnlearn`, is the honest report of how stable each arrow is. Cycles can be handled by unrolling in time, as on the dynamic slide, or with cyclic structural causal models, whose equilibrium semantics is more delicate (Bongers and colleagues, *Annals of Statistics*, 2021).
:::

## Two implementations {.smaller #sec-bn-packages}

| | [`bnlearn`](https://www.bnlearn.com/) | [pyAgrum](https://pyagrum.readthedocs.io/) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Language | R | Python, on the C++ library aGrUM |
| Structure search | The long catalogue: PC, Grow-Shrink, IAMB, MMPC, hill-climbing, tabu, MMHC, RSMAX2 | Hill-climbing, tabu, MIIC and 3off2; PC and FCI in recent releases |
| Inference | Conditional queries. Exact for discrete and Gaussian networks; approximate otherwise | Lazy propagation and other junction-tree methods, plus sampling. Exact inference is the main engine |
| Also | Bootstrap of the graph, interventions, counterfactuals | Influence diagrams, credal networks, Markov random fields |
| Where the cost sits | Conditional-independence tests, which grow with the conditioning set | The junction tree. A large clique dominates the exact query |

Neither search supplies a causal reading by itself.

::: {.notes}
bnlearn is the structure-learning catalogue behind labels such as MMPC and RSMAX. pyAgrum is the inference engine, and it also holds influence diagrams and credal nets. Do not quote a speed ratio between the packages. Tabu against constraint-based searches was Scutari's comparison of algorithms, already on the search slide.
:::
